skyline.text: Why the best peo­ple need other ex­cel­lent peo­ple around them
Why play­ing at state­hood is no train­ing for co­er­cive power
Amit Varma’s cure for writer’s block: two or three es­says

brief.head: Still rolling
brief.text: There are no film cans any more, but the pro­ducer still says “rolling”. Conventions like the QWERTY key­board, Amit Varma said, stick long after their rea­sons van­ish. {008-C01}

brief.head: Capital follows talent
brief.text: Open, di­verse cities draw en­trepreneurs, artists and gay and les­bian com­mu­ni­ties, Varma said, cit­ing Richard Florida. Capital then chases that tal­ent, and a vir­tu­ous cycle be­gins. {008-C05}

brief.head: Why do they leave?
brief.text: IIT grad­u­ates who go abroad[[x4]] are mak­ing ra­tio­nal choices, Varma ar­gued. The real ques­tion is why India chases good peo­ple away in­stead of build­ing cen­tres of ex­cel­lence. {008-C08}

brief.head: A deep bench
brief.text: Want a cute 20-man team? Finland will do, Ajay Shah said. Want 2,000 peo­ple? Come to India, where the depth of the bench is phe­nom­e­nal. {008-C09}

brief.head: Guns make bad states
brief.text: Freedom won by armed strug­gle tends to go badly, Shah said, be­cause vi­o­lence lifts gen­er­als, not philoso­pher kings. India’s one piece of magic was ahimsa. {008-C14}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on where talent flourishes
lead.head: Genius loves company

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 8

body: Amit Varma once turned down a Nobel lau­re­ate[[x1]]. When Abhijit Banerjee won the prize, his pub­lish­ers of­fered him for Varma’s pod­cast that same week, but for only one hour. Varma asked for at least two. When they re­fused, he said no. {008-S01}

One hour, he rea­soned, would have got him the stan­dard ques­tions about RCTs. Three would have let him go back to the 1960s, when his fa­ther stud­ied at Presidency College under Banerjee’s fa­ther, Deepak Banerjee.
The story led to a col­umn on this episode’s ques­tion: why does tal­ent gather in a few places, soft­ware en­gi­neers in Silicon Valley, film­mak­ers in Bombay?
Banerjee went to Presidency College, then JNU, then Harvard. Varma’s con­tro­ver­sial claim was that Harvard was crit­i­cal to his de­vel­op­ment.
## The ten-dollar les­son
His ev­i­dence was Michael Kremer’s 1993 paper on the O-ring, the $10 part whose fail­ure de­stroyed the $3.2 bil­lion Challenger shut­tle in 1986.
In com­plex work, Varma ex­plained, qual­ity mul­ti­plies rather than adds. Ten peo­ple at 0.99 pro­duce 9.05; at 0.95, 5.99; at 0.90, just 3.49. {008-C02}
“So a small dif­fer­ence in tal­ent leads to a mas­sive dif­fer­ence in out­put and pro­duc­tiv­ity,” he said. The best peo­ple there­fore gain most by work­ing be­side each other.

Ajay Shah agreed, with caveats. Where parts are stan­dard­ised, as in a car or in soft­ware, peo­ple can work apart. The hard part is agree­ing who does what: “The con­tract­ing is a big­ger prob­lem than the ac­tual work.” {008-C04}
## Lost ge­niuses
Shah also thought Indian mid­dle-class par­ents over­state how make-or-break clus­ters are. Ramanujan, cut off in a re­mote cor­ner of Tamil Nadu, re­built 19th-century math­e­mat­ics on his own.

Varma an­swered with Viswanathan Anand, who con­quered a chess world dom­i­nated by the Soviet school with­out its train­ing. It was, he said, “like some­one tak­ing a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race and win­ning the damn thing”. {008-S06}
But out­liers in­spire; they do not make pol­icy. “There are count­less Ramanujans and Anands who have been lost to us who are un­seen,” Varma said.
Clusters can also cor­rupt. Bombay, he said, can take bright small-town kids steeped in cul­ture and, within a year, flat­ten them into shal­low party talk.
## A state in re­hearsal

The sec­ond half turned to the state. In McLeod Ganj, Shah walked through the Central Tibetan Administration, a gov­ern­ment in exile funded by do­na­tions, with no tax­a­tion and no co­er­cive power.
Could it be train­ing wheels for a free Tibet? No, he ar­gued: no­body learns to wield co­er­cive power by play-acting. {008-C13}

India, he said, should build reg­u­la­tors as pa­tiently as it builds bridges, with de­sign, pro­cesses and staged pow­ers, rather than no­ti­fy­ing a law and ex­pect­ing a hand­ful of peo­ple to per­form overnight.

Varma was gloomier. India’s state, he said, was de­signed to rule rather than serve, a con­tin­u­a­tion of the colo­nial one. Independent India, he pointed out, taxed salt far more than the British Empire had.

Shah’s reply was hope as an in­tel­lec­tual project. A cen­tury ago, he said, India’s chat­ter­ing classes ar­gued over what free India would look like, and got the state wrong. Now is the time for re­search.
Varma, for his part, said the the­ory ex­plained why he spends so much time with Shah: “That’s why I like to sit with you, be­cause it can only make me a bet­ter thinker and a bet­ter per­son.”

second.label: Physics at Göttingen
second.head: Bad apple, top class
second.deck: Amit Varma on how Göttingen took an unhappy misfit to another level
body: At school and col­lege, Oppenheimer was un­happy and fit­ted in nowhere. He even tried to poi­son his physics teacher, Amit Varma said, by putting poi­son in an apple[[x2]]. {008-S03}
Then he went to the University of Göttingen. He was taught by Max Born, who, Varma said, coined the term quan­tum me­chan­ics. His class­mates were of the cal­i­bre of Dirac and John von Neumann.

For Varma, it was the O-ring the­ory at work in a sin­gle life: among peers of the high­est cal­i­bre, the mis­fit went to an en­tirely dif­fer­ent level. If you are lucky in a par­tic­u­lar place and time, he said, a con­gre­ga­tion can pro­duce “an ex­po­nen­tial ex­plo­sion of tal­ent”. {#gottingen}

quote.text: He has class­mates of the cal­i­bre of Dirac and John von Neumann, and he goes to an en­tirely dif­fer­ent level.

third.head: Comrades out, brokers in

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Warsaw stock exchange

body: In Warsaw, Ajay Shah heard a story. After com­mu­nism ended, Poland took the of­fice of the Communist Party, the big­gest and most pow­er­ful build­ing in the city, and turned it into the stock ex­change. {008-S10}
“They were mak­ing a state­ment that we are fin­ished with this stuff and we now want to learn to be a cap­i­tal­ist coun­try,” Shah said.

Having lived under com­mu­nism and know­ing how bad it was, Eastern Europeans wanted to run far from it, he ar­gued. Joining the European Union helped too: it came with 20,000 pages of draft laws[[x3]] and treaty re­stric­tions. {#eu}

Russia, by con­trast, pri­va­tised com­pa­nies and asked mar­kets to ap­pear overnight, with Jeff Sachs among those push­ing, but paid too lit­tle at­ten­tion to the state. “Freedom is coded into laws and state in­sti­tu­tions,” Shah said. {008-C15}

box.title: The paper behind the episode
box.text: Michael Kremer shared the Nobel with Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo. His sem­i­nal 1993 paper, *The O-Ring Theory of Economic Development*, ex­plains with sim­ple mul­ti­pli­ca­tion why small dif­fer­ences in skill cre­ate huge dif­fer­ences in out­put and pay. {008-R02}

sections.label: The first idea
sections.head: Small gaps, giant sums
sections.caption: the O-ring theory of talent
body: In 1986 the space shut­tle Challenger, a $3.2 bil­lion project, ex­ploded be­cause a $10 O-ring failed. Michael Kremer named his sem­i­nal 1993 paper after that flimsy part, and Amit Varma built his case on it. {008-S02}
The les­son, Varma said, is not the triv­ial point that a chain is only as strong as its weak­est link. It is about the in­ter­play be­tween tal­ent, pro­duc­tiv­ity and wages.

In com­plex work, qual­ity mul­ti­plies. Ten peo­ple each per­form­ing at 0.99 pro­duce an out­put of 9.05. At 0.95, it­self in­cred­i­bly tal­ented, the out­put falls to 5.99. At 0.90 it is just 3.49. {008-C02}
## Worth twice the money

So some­one at 0.99 can be paid twice or thrice as much as some­one at 0.95, though the gap barely shows. The ef­fect is strong­est, Varma said, where qual­ity mat­ters more than quan­tity, since one great nov­el­ist beats three medi­ocre ones, and where a task has thou­sands of links that must all hold.

That is why the best peo­ple seek each other out, and why Harvard mat­tered to Abhijit Banerjee. Elite col­leges do offer cre­den­tials and sort­ing, Varma granted. But they also put you among some of the finest minds.
~ For a fuller ac­count, he pointed to Tyler Cowen’s Marginal Revolution University video on the model, which he called fan­tas­tic. {#cowen}

quote.text: You need to be around other stag­ger­ingly tal­ented and qual­i­fied peo­ple to get a full ex­pres­sion of your abil­i­ties.

sections.label: The rejoinder
sections.head: Trust first, work anywhere
sections.caption: plug compatibility and trust
body: Ajay Shah came at the O-ring prob­lem from the fac­tory floor. Mass man­u­fac­tur­ing, he said, solved it with stan­dard­ised parts. A car con­tains 10,000 parts and works flaw­lessly be­cause every ball bear­ing sits within very tight tol­er­ances. {#car}

Software does the same with APIs. “That damn thing had bet­ter just work,” Shah said. Where the in­ter­face is de­fined, two peo­ple need never talk. A movie is the op­po­site: hun­dreds of peo­ple in im­pre­cise, poorly de­fined re­la­tion­ships. {008-C03}

Distance from a clus­ter is no death sen­tence ei­ther. Cut off in a re­mote cor­ner of Tamil Nadu, Ramanujan set about re­build­ing the math­e­mat­ics of the 19th cen­tury on his own. The early University of Chicago, far from the East Coast, bred in­de­pen­dent think­ing. {008-S05}
## The hand­shake prob­lem

The real limit, Shah ar­gued, is con­tract­ing: agree­ing who does what, how de­ci­sions are made and how re­sources are shared. That needs peo­ple who know and trust each other, which is the magic of London, New York and Cambridge, Massachusetts. After that, the work can hap­pen any­where. {008-C04}
~ In the hu­man­i­ties and so­cial sci­ences, he added, “au­then­tic­ity is king”. {008-C07} To know Indian eco­nom­ics you must be in India; abroad, he felt “a cer­tain empti­ness”.

quote.text: I will sug­gest that the con­tract­ing is a big­ger prob­lem than the ac­tual work.

art.caption: Amit Varma on plug compatibility and trust

sections.label: Training wheels
sections.head: No taxes, no training
sections.caption: the government in exile
body: Ajay Shah’s T-shirt bore the name of the Tibet Museum in McLeod Ganj, which he called a re­ally great mu­seum. It sits in­side the com­plex of the Central Tibetan Administration: “a liv­ing, breath­ing gov­ern­ment in exile”. {008-S09}

Shah was proud that India has been kind to Tibetan refugees, even when it was costly. But the CTA, with its Department of Finance and Department of Home, runs on do­na­tions. It has no tax­a­tion and no co­er­cive power.

Could this wannabe state be train­ing wheels for a free Tibet? Shah thought not. “Coercive power is a poi­son,”[[x6]] he said, and play-acting is no prepa­ra­tion. Tidy de­part­ments might even lull peo­ple into “iso­mor­phic mimicry”[[x7]]. {008-C13}
## How new states fare
When Charles de Gaulle led the French gov­ern­ment in exile in London, Shah doubted he set up a de­part­ment of health; he fo­cused on get­ting to a free France. {#degaulle}

New states, Shah said, have mostly fared badly, worst where free­dom came through armed strug­gle. The suc­cess sto­ries are in Eastern Europe. For China, the best hope is the in­sti­tu­tional DNA of Taiwan, not the CTA.
~ Amit Varma found the play-acting ad­mirable but poignant: min­istries that could not pos­si­bly look like those of an ac­tual free Tibet.

quote.text: You don’t de­velop state ca­pa­bil­ity with­out ac­tu­ally fight­ing with the bat­tle of the evil that is co­er­cive power.

sections.label: The Indian lesson
sections.head: Regulators are bridges too
sections.caption: building a regulator like a bridge
body: India, Ajay Shah said, ac­cepts that a bridge takes time: project man­age­ment, many hands, and a min­is­ter cut­ting the rib­bon two or five years later. “But no­body ex­pects a zero day lag be­tween the de­ci­sion to have a bridge and the bridge.” {008-C16}

A new reg­u­la­tor, such as a food safety au­thor­ity, de­serves the same pa­tience: or­gan­i­sa­tional de­sign, writ­ten pro­cesses, trained staff, IT sys­tems and re­peated re­view of checks and bal­ances, with pow­ers no­ti­fied in stages. Launched overnight, it goes into fire­fight­ing from day three and never re­cov­ers.

The clos­est India came, he said, was the plan MS Sahoo and Ravi Narain led for the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India[[x8]]. “In re­al­ity, the law was no­ti­fied and overnight five peo­ple were ex­pected to per­form.” {008-S11}
## Is decay in­evitable?

Amit Varma asked whether all in­sti­tu­tions must de­grade. No, Shah said. An institution’s DNA lies in its law, and co­er­cive power, like a nu­clear re­ac­tor, needs enough cladding. “Most of our Indian laws are based on an op­ti­mistic read­ing of human be­ings.” {008-C17}
~ The usual Indian re­sponse to a fail­ing agency, he said, is to de­mand a bet­ter CEO, a prim­i­tive great man the­ory. The real de­bate should be over checks and bal­ances. {008-C18}

quote.text: So we are in that R&D phase of fig­ur­ing out what a suc­cess­ful, pros­per­ous India would look like.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on building a regulator like a bridge

sections.label: Amit’s pick
sections.head: Write clearly, think better
sections.caption: Orwell and clear writing
body: Amit Varma’s rec­om­men­da­tion was not *Animal Farm* or *1984* but George Orwell’s col­lected es­says, which present his work in chrono­log­i­cal order: a look at Orwell the thinker. {008-R15}

Whenever he got stuck on a col­umn, Varma said, he would read two or three pieces, what­ever their sub­ject. The clar­ity of Orwell’s lan­guage and the rhythms he builds “would free some­thing within me”.
## Writing is re­search

Writing and think­ing feed each other both ways, he ar­gued. “If you force your­self to write clearly, you are forced to think bet­ter[[x9]] be­cause you can­not hide be­hind ab­stract words or vague jar­gon.” {008-C20}

He cited Joan Didion[[x10]]: “I don’t know what I think until I write it down.” {#didion} Deirdre McCloskey, whose *Economical Writing* he also rec­om­mended, holds, in his para­phrase, that the writ­ing is re­search.

Ajay Shah rec­om­mended a story about the nov­el­ist Cormac McCarthy clean­ing up a sci­en­tific paper, and re­cited from mem­ory lines of a poem Orwell slipped into an essay. “Insane mem­ory,” said Varma. {008-J20}

~ Shah’s own pick built on the O-ring talk: William Easterly’s *The Elusive Quest for Growth*, which knocks the fad­dish ideas out of de­vel­op­ment. {008-R22} Varma added Easterly’s *The White Man’s Burden*.

quote.text: Saints should al­ways be judged guilty until they are proved in­no­cent
quote.who: George Orwell, as read by Amit Varma

quote.text: The ques­tion then is that why are they hav­ing to go abroad? What can we do to cre­ate cen­tres of ex­cel­lence here so that peo­ple feel in­spired, peo­ple feel happy?

p3.title: Where talent goes
p3.deck: Chess prodigies, small-town artists and a paper written by strangers

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Viswanathan Anand and the Soviet school
stories.head: The boy who skipped Soviet school
body: Some time in the 1930s, as Amit Varma guessed, a top Soviet func­tionary named Nikolai Krylenko de­manded “shock brigades of chess play­ers” and “a five-year plan for chess”. He could not have said it later, Varma noted: Stalin purged him in 1938. {#krylenko}

The Soviet Union wanted to prove its su­pe­ri­or­ity through a game of the brain. Chess was taught in schools the way maths is, giv­ing a huge pool from which tal­ent was trained sys­tem­at­i­cally up to grand­mas­ter level. The Soviet school came to mean[[x12]] a shared way of think­ing, heuris­tics handed from trainer to pupil.

Varma’s friend Devangshu Datta[[x11]], who played se­ri­ous chess for India in the 1980s, likened fac­ing East Europeans to pit­ting self-taught HSC-level maths stu­dents against post­grad­u­ates. In the post-mortem, the op­po­nent would ex­plain that his trainer had taught him how to play that struc­ture. “And you’d be like, shit.” {008-J06}
Ajay Shah sup­plied the chess world’s in­side joke for that gap: “as every Russian school­boy knows”. {008-J15}

Into this world came Viswanathan Anand. In his for­ma­tive years, in the Philippines as Varma re­calls it, a TV chess pro­gramme set puz­zles. Anand kept send­ing the right an­swers until, Varma re­mem­bers, they asked him to stop en­ter­ing and of­fered him all the chess books he wanted. {008-J05}

Without Soviet train­ing, Anand rose to dom­i­nate and later be­came world cham­pion. “The metaphor I draw for it is like some­one tak­ing a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race and win­ning the damn thing,” Varma said. {008-S06}
~ Yet Varma calls Anand an out­lier, not a model: for every Ramanujan or Anand who made it, count­less oth­ers were lost.
stories.why: A sys­tem that gath­ers and trains tal­ent builds a store of knowl­edge that a lone ge­nius must re­build from scratch. That makes Anand’s feat stag­ger­ing, and makes him an ex­cep­tion to ad­mire rather than a pol­icy to copy. {008-C06}
stories.postscript: Varma’s other image for it: “like win­ning Wimbledon today with a wooden racket”.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Anand and the Soviet school

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what Bombay does to small-town talent
stories.head: Big city, small talk
body: Bollywood, Amit Varma said, is a place of great op­por­tu­nity, but Bombay is also “where dreams come to die and art comes to be cor­rupted”. {008-S07}
On an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*, Vikram Sathaye told him about bright kids from small towns in Maharashtra who ar­rive steeped in cul­ture, read­ing Vijay Tendulkar, deep into local forms.

In Bombay they meet shal­low peo­ple. A year later, Sathaye runs into one of them at a party, some­one who had dis­cussed Tendulkar with him the year be­fore. Now it is: “Dude, how are you doing? Let’s go chill.”

~ Ajay Shah coun­tered that 99% of ev­ery­thing is crass and shal­low, in Bollywood or Silicon Valley alike. Varma’s point was dif­fer­ent: a good per­son can come to Bollywood and pro­duce bad work be­cause there are “in­cen­tives for medi­ocrity”. {008-C12}
stories.why: Clusters do not only lift tal­ent up. Their in­cen­tives and sta­tus games can also flat­ten it, and the pres­sure to fit in can strip away what made a small-town new­comer dis­tinc­tive.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Bombay’s shallow end

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Vinay Singhal’s streaming bet
stories.head: Haryanvi kids come home
body: Vinay Singhal de­scribed his app, Stage.in[[x13]], to Amit Varma as Netflix for Bharat: not in lan­guages like Hindi or Punjabi but in di­alects, Haryanvi, Bhojpuri and, Varma thinks, now Rajasthani.

Traditional ven­ture cap­i­tal­ists told him it would never work. He charged Netflix rates any­way and has, Varma thinks, some 300,000 sub­scribers by now. {#subscribers} The VCs are flock­ing, and there was a big fund­ing round last year.

Singhal also de­scribed what he called the re­verse mi­gra­tion from Bollywood. {008-S08} Haryanvi kids who once headed to Bombay to make films are com­ing back, to a Haryanvi film in­dus­try of some 3,000 peo­ple. {#haryanvi}

~ Cities drive human progress, Varma said, but they ho­mogenise[[x14]]: a Bhojpuri speaker in a Hindi city may drop the di­alect to avoid seem­ing “vernie”. Technology and cap­i­tal­ism can now push the other way.

quote.text: One of the side ef­fects is that ho­mogeni­sa­tion hap­pens, you can lose di­alects, you can lose sub­cul­tures.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the reverse migration

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on research across borders
stories.head: Strangers on a mailing list
body: Ajay Shah’s good friend Achim Zeileis is a statis­ti­cian in Vienna. Shah, Ila Patnaik and Zeileis struck up a con­ver­sa­tion over mail­ing lists and re­alised they were chas­ing dif­fer­ent pieces of a cor­re­lated puz­zle. {008-S04}

They wrote a paper to­gether, one Shah counts among the nice pa­pers of his life, with­out ever meet­ing. “We got all the way to our first paper with­out even video calls, just on email and SVN,” he said.
Only later did they meet, and it was great. Their paper *What is the New Chinese Currency Regime?* is among Shah’s rec­om­men­da­tions.

~ Still, Shah said, re­mote teams need human rap­port. Without meet­ing, hu­mour is “so dan­ger­ous it can just be mis­un­der­stood”, or ev­ery­one turns into au­toma­tons writ­ing “hor­ri­ble ChatGPT lan­guage”. {#humour}
stories.why: Serious re­search can be done at in­ter­net scale once the work is de­fined. What still needs a room, Shah ar­gued, is the trust that lets peo­ple agree who does what. {008-C04}

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 8. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: George Orwell (Cassowary Colorizations, CC BY 2.0); Michael Kremer (Harvard University, CC BY-SA 4.0); J. Robert Oppenheimer (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Abhijit Banerjee (Sriya Sarkar, CC BY 4.0); Charles de Gaulle (The National Archives UK, No restrictions); Joan Didion (Kathleen Ballard, Los Angeles Times, CC BY 4.0); William Easterly (Jerry Bauer, CC BY-SA 4.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Why Abhijit Banerjee Had to Go Abroad to Achieve Glory
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It sets out the episode’s core claim: tal­ent con­gre­gates, and Harvard was crit­i­cal to Banerjee’s de­vel­op­ment.

shelf.title: The O-Ring Theory of Economic Development
shelf.creator: Michael Kremer
shelf.why: It ex­plains with sim­ple mul­ti­pli­ca­tion why small dif­fer­ences in skill cre­ate huge dif­fer­ences in out­put and pay, and why the best peo­ple clus­ter to­gether.

shelf.title: The O-Ring Model (Marginal Revolution University video)
shelf.creator: Tyler Cowen
shelf.why: He calls it fan­tas­tic and says it ex­plains the model in de­tail, bet­ter than his own on-air sum­mary.

shelf.title: My Hero, Oppenheimer (Episode 5)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Fuller back­ground on Oppenheimer, the episode’s prime ex­am­ple of a mis­fit who flour­ished once he was among peers of his cal­i­bre.

shelf.title: The Rise of the Creative Class
shelf.creator: Richard Florida
shelf.why: It ar­gues that growth fol­lows cre­ative con­gre­ga­tion: open, di­verse cities draw en­trepreneurs, artists and gay and les­bian com­mu­ni­ties, and cap­i­tal then chases that tal­ent.

shelf.title: The Adda at the End of the Universe (Episode 309 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s adda with friends Vikram Sathaye and Roshan Abbas, the source of sto­ries he keeps re­turn­ing to: the friend who changed his mind about liv­ing long, healthy lives, and tal­ented small-town kids los­ing their depth in Bombay, a re­minder that clus­ters can cor­rupt as well as up­lift.

shelf.title: The Refreshing Audacity of Vinay Singhal (Episode 291 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Entrepreneur Vinay Singhal on build­ing Stage, a di­alect-first stream­ing busi­ness that proved scep­ti­cal VCs wrong and is push­ing back against Hindi’s pres­sure on India’s di­alects, in­clud­ing a ‘re­verse mi­gra­tion from Bollywood’.

shelf.title: Stage.in
shelf.creator: Vinay Singhal
shelf.why: Vinay Singhal’s ‘Netflix for Bharat’, stream­ing con­tent in di­alects like Haryanvi and Bhojpuri: Amit’s live ex­am­ple of tech­nol­ogy and long-tail mar­kets re­vers­ing the ho­mogeni­sa­tion of di­alects.

shelf.title: The Tamilian Gentleman Who Took on the World
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s piece on Viswanathan Anand ris­ing with­out the Soviet school’s sys­tem­atic train­ing, like tak­ing a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race, which shows how ex­tra­or­di­nary his world-championship ca­reer was.

shelf.title: Marching For Salt
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s sur­pris­ing point that in­de­pen­dent India taxed salt far more than the British did, ev­i­dence that the free­dom strug­gle is in­com­plete, and more of his take on Gandhi.

shelf.title: What is the New Chinese Currency Regime?
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah, Achim Zeileis and Ila Patnaik
shelf.why: It is Ajay’s ex­am­ple of se­ri­ous re­search pro­duced by a team spread across coun­tries.

shelf.title: The Tibet Museum, McLeod Ganj
shelf.why: Unlike many Indian mu­se­ums it is done well, with arte­facts that trig­ger the mind.

shelf.title: Building the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India
shelf.creator: MS Sahoo and Ravi Narain
shelf.why: Ajay calls it a mile­stone in India’s jour­ney: a real plan for build­ing an or­gan­i­sa­tion that will wield co­er­cive power, even though it was largely ig­nored in prac­tice.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Essays
shelf.creator: George Orwell
shelf.why: Orwell’s non­fic­tion, which Amit prefers to the nov­els: a chrono­log­i­cal look at Orwell the thinker, who banged out three or four bril­liant col­umns a week.

shelf.title: Politics and the English Language
shelf.creator: George Orwell
shelf.why: Orwell’s primer on clear writ­ing, which shows the link runs both ways: writ­ing clearly forces you to think clearly, and jar­gon is where mud­dled think­ing hides.

shelf.title: Why I Write
shelf.creator: George Orwell
shelf.why: A com­pan­ion piece to Amit’s seg­ment on Orwell, clear writ­ing and the link be­tween writ­ing and think­ing.

shelf.title: Reflections on Gandhi
shelf.creator: George Orwell
shelf.why: It shows what a beau­ti­ful writer and thinker Orwell was: scep­ti­cal of saint­hood yet fair, and alert to the shrewd, able per­son in­side Gandhi.

shelf.title: Joan Didion’s writing
shelf.creator: Joan Didion
shelf.why: Her line ‘I don’t know what I think until I write it down’ sums up writ­ing as a way of dis­cov­er­ing your own thoughts.

shelf.title: How Cormac McCarthy Became a Copy-Editor for Scientific Books and One of the Most Influential Articles in Economics
shelf.creator: Josh Jones
shelf.why: The story of nov­el­ist Cormac McCarthy clean­ing up a sci­en­tific paper, which Ajay says ev­ery­one in academia should study as a les­son in how re­search should be writ­ten.

shelf.title: Economical Writing
shelf.creator: Deirdre McCloskey
shelf.why: McCloskey shows how to write about eco­nom­ics, or any com­plex sub­ject, so that lay read­ers find it clear and in­ter­est­ing: ex­actly what Amit’s stu­dents from jar­gon-rewarding fields like so­ci­ol­ogy and an­thro­pol­ogy need.

shelf.title: The Elusive Quest for Growth
shelf.creator: William Easterly
shelf.why: Easterly knocks out the fad­dish ideas that have dam­aged de­vel­op­ment and leaves you ask­ing what your the­ory of growth re­ally is.

shelf.title: The White Man’s Burden
shelf.creator: William Easterly
shelf.why: Easterly on why the West’s ef­forts to aid the rest have done so much ill and so lit­tle good: es­sen­tial read­ing on how in­cen­tives dis­tort de­vel­op­ment work, by a clear writer and great thinker.

laughs.text: Ajay, ex­plain­ing that some work needs a min­i­mum team size, of­fers ‘triv­ial pro­duc­tion projects like some YouTube pod­cast with an eclec­tic name, ev­ery­thing is everything’ as what you can make with es­sen­tially no team.
Amit scolds Ajay for hurt­ing their pro­ducer Vartika’s feel­ings with talk of tiny teams. Ajay protests: ‘it’s a three-man team and you know we couldn’t have made a movie even if we wanted.’
On how much time he needs with a guest: Amit asked for two or three hours with Banerjee, ‘and today of course I would in­sist on five hours or noth­ing.’
Amit notes that Orwell, like Bastiat, died at 49, ‘which is my age right now. So may I some­how reach the end of December, I’ll be very happy.’

Young Anand kept win­ning the puz­zle con­tests on a Philippine TV chess show until, as Amit re­mem­bers it, they called and said: ‘Look, you’re win­ning ev­ery­thing, just stop en­ter­ing, we’ll give you all the chess books you want once and for all.’
Devangshu Datta on fac­ing Soviet-trained play­ers: the op­po­nent would ex­plain in the post-mortem that his trainer taught him how to play that struc­ture, ‘and you’d be like, shit.’
Amit’s im­ages for Anand’s feat: ‘like some­one tak­ing a Maruti 800 into a Formula One race and win­ning the damn thing’, or ‘win­ning Wimbledon today with a wooden racket.’
Ajay turns Orwell’s dic­tum into ‘Podcasts should be like a win­dow­pane.’ Amit ex­plains the source: Orwell’s line that good prose should be like a win­dow­pane.
Ajay: Orwell mat­ters more ‘now that we know that his­tory did not end’, a nod to the ‘end of history’ idea. Amit: ‘And now that nine­teen eighty four is ap­proach­ing.’
Freddy, the plush toy on the table, is named after Amit’s hero Frédéric Bastiat and after Friedrich Hayek: ‘two Freddies, he car­ries both of them within him.’

‘As every Russian school­boy knows’: Ajay’s chess-world in­side joke for things that seem deep to out­siders but are com­mon knowl­edge to Soviet-trained kids. The phrase has spread far be­yond chess.

Sturgeon’s Law, cited by Amit as ‘ninety-eight per­cent of ev­ery­thing is crap’. Ajay’s ver­sion: ‘99% of ev­ery­thing is crass, shal­low bullshit’, whether Bollywood, Indian star­tups or Silicon Valley.

Orwell lines re­cited from mem­ory by Ajay, de­scrib­ing the mood of the 1930s: ‘It is for­bid­den to dream again; we maim our hopes or hide them. The horses are made of chromium steel, and lit­tle fat men shall ride them.’ Amit’s re­ac­tion: ‘Insane mem­ory.’

From Orwell’s ‘Reflections on Gandhi’, read by Amit: ‘Saints should al­ways be judged guilty until they are proved innocent’, and that in­side the saint ‘there was a very shrewd, able per­son who could, if he had cho­sen, have been a bril­liant suc­cess as a lawyer, an ad­min­is­tra­tor, or per­haps even a busi­ness­man.’
